clue.text: Like a form of English coming from mouth

definitions.meaning: ... English is the accent of the Thames ... region around London, so the word describes that form of speech
the wide tidal mouth of a river where it meets the sea

explanation.surface: A dialect of English said to come straight out of someone's mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming from' is a link. Estuary English is a British accent of London and the south-east, between Cockney and standard speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The tidal stretch where a river widens into the sea is its mouth, and the London accent takes its name from the Thames one.

clue.text: Female with others drumming up support

definitions.text: Female with others drumming up support

parts.words: Female with others drumming up support
parts.note: read literally: a girl marching in a band with drummers, twirling a baton to cheer on a team

explanation.surface: A woman joining a group campaign to win backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drumming up support' sounds like canvassing, but it is literal: she marches with drummers and cheers a team on.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton-twirling girl leads a marching band at parades and games, rousing the crowd.

clue.text: The last thing you expect at a soccer match

definitions.text: The last thing you expect at a soccer match

parts.words: The last thing you expect at a soccer match
parts.note: read literally: the final thing you wait for at a game is its outcome, not something improbable

explanation.surface: Something very unlikely to happen at a football game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last thing you expect' is an idiom for something improbable; read literally it is the final score you await.
explanation.definitionFit: At a football match the final score is the outcome everyone waits for at the end.

clue.text: Character who is lacking, having no heart, I fancy

indicators.note: to fancy is to imagine or invent, so the letters of the words before are freely reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes a cold, unfeeling character, adding 'I fancy' as an aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no heart' looks like a deletion instruction, but those words themselves are the fodder: rearrange NOHEART plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: A protagonist who lacks heroic virtues such as courage or idealism is the classic flawed lead.

clue.text: Novel route via Suez or cape of good hope?

definitions.meaning: a book by E. M. Forster, published in 1924

definitions.text: route via Suez or cape of good hope?
definitions.meaning: a sea voyage to the subcontinent went through the Suez Canal or round the southern tip of Africa

explanation.surface: Comparing two old shipping routes east, one through Egypt and one round Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The lower-case 'cape of good hope' hides the Cape of Good Hope, the southern tip of Africa that ships rounded before the canal opened.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's famous book about British rule shares its title with a voyage to the Raj by either sea route.

clue.text: One has sweet things in store for school pupils

definitions.text: One has sweet things in store for school pupils

parts.words: One has sweet things in store for school pupils
parts.note: read literally: a kiosk that stocks sweets and sells them to children at school

explanation.surface: Someone has pleasant surprises waiting for the children at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in store' suggests something coming later; here it means literally held in a shop. A British school shop selling sweets and snacks is a familiar institution.
explanation.definitionFit: A small shop at or near a British school sells confectionery and snacks to the pupils.

clue.text: Greetings from a nasty place that has nothing

definitions.note: a plural noun, while the answer is a single word of greeting usable as an interjection

parts.note: the underworld of torment is the nastiest place imaginable
the letter O looks like a zero, meaning nothing

explanation.surface: Someone receives a hello from a horrible empty place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' and 'that has' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A word said on meeting someone is a salutation, one of the commonest greetings.

clue.text: Characters involved in a tirade somehow glow

indicators.note: the letters arrive at their new order in some unstated way, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A ranting speech that somehow makes someone shine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters involved in' is a link pointing to the letters of A TIRADE, which 'somehow' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: To give off light or heat in all directions is to shine or emit warmth.

clue.text: Slip out from the class finally, having got cloak

indicators.note: the final letter of each of the two words before is taken

parts.note: a cape is a sleeveless cloak

explanation.surface: A pupil sneaks out of class at the end, grabbing a coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the last letter of both 'the' and 'class'; 'from' and 'having got' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To slip out is to get away unnoticed, to break free.

clue.text: Bill gets pass and two poor grades — hardly merits this!

annotationWithheld.why: Bill gets pass and two poor grades — hardly merits this! (8): AC (bill) + COL (pass) + D, E (poor grades) gives ACCOLDE; no clue word supplies the remaining A, and no web source gives the setter's parse
annotationWithheld.clue: Bill gets pass and two poor grades — hardly merits this!

clue.text: Report of traffic jams? They'll supply written news

indicators.note: a report is something spoken, so the words that follow are said aloud

parts.note: lines of stationary cars can be called auto queues

explanation.surface: A traffic report, followed by a mention of where the written news comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: AUTO QUEUES (car queues) sounds like the answer; screens of scrolling text let newsreaders read the news.
explanation.definitionFit: Teleprompter screens show presenters the script they read out on air.

clue.text: Hit associated with a new advertising catchphrase

parts.note: to slog is to hit hard, especially in cricket

explanation.surface: A hit song linked with a fresh advertising jingle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'associated with' is a link joining the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A short memorable motto used to sell a product is the marketer's catchy phrase.

clue.text: Teenager brewed drink

indicators.note: brewing stirs and mixes ingredients, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A teenager has brewed a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewed' rearranges the eight letters of TEENAGER.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfermented leaf infusion popular in East Asia is a common hot beverage.

clue.text: Cricket deliveries go both ways — deceptive things!

parts.note: the word go written forwards and then backwards
falsehoods are things meant to deceive

explanation.surface: A remark about cricket bowling that swings both ways and deceives batsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket these are balls from a leg-spinner that turn the opposite way to the one the batsman expects.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrong'un in cricket is a disguised spin ball that turns the opposite way, a classic deceptive delivery.

clue.text: Chemist's small room less quiet when the roof's come off

definitions.note: read as Chemist is, the possessive standing for the verb

parts.note: lav is short for lavatory, the smallest room in the house

indicators.note: in a down entry the roof is the top letter, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: noisier means less quiet

explanation.surface: A chemist's tiny room gets noisier once its roof is torn off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the roof's come off' drops the first letter of NOISIER, leaving OISIER. Antoine Lavoisier was the 18th-century French chemist who named oxygen.
explanation.definitionFit: The French scientist who identified oxygen and hydrogen is called the father of modern chemistry.

clue.text: Elegant young socialite floating with the wind?

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, a young woman entering society
something borne aloft by moving air is on the air

explanation.surface: A stylish debutante drifting along on the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the loose phrase 'floating with the wind' for ON AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Suave and stylishly confident describes a charming, graceful manner.

clue.text: A daughter here given holy books, as befits disciple

parts.note: taken as written
NT is the New Testament, a set of holy books

explanation.surface: A daughter is given scripture, as suits a follower of the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given' and 'as befits' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower or supporter of a leader or creed is one of its devotees.

clue.text: Soft? About time to be brave!

indicators.note: the soft word goes about, around, the time letter

parts.note: doughy means soft and pasty

explanation.surface: Being called soft prompts a challenge: time to show some courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Doughty is an old word for valiant and resolute, as in a stout-hearted fighter.

clue.text: The Yorkshireman who destroys machinery, they say, is someone on a journey!

indicators.note: points to what is said aloud

parts.note: Yorkshire dialect shortens the to t', so the wrecker becomes t'wrecker

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire machine-breaker is called a traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire speech famously clips 'the' to t'; T'WRECKER, a wrecker being one who destroys things, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A traveller making a long, arduous trip on foot is a hiker or wayfarer.

clue.text: Like certain commercial transactions of fellow directors

parts.note: taken as written
a company's directors form its board

explanation.surface: Describing business deals made among members of a company's board.
explanation.walkthrough: Off-board trading is dealing in shares outside a formal stock exchange.
explanation.definitionFit: Trades done outside an official exchange are called this, the market term for over-the-counter dealing.

clue.text: A number believe in America

definitions.meaning: American usage for to think or reckon, as in I guess so

explanation.surface: A count of people who believe in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'believe in America' looks like faith in the country; it means 'believe' in American speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A digit is a numeral, and Americans say they reckon something is so using the same word.

clue.text: Exactly the words to describe Kipling's stories

definitions.meaning: precisely, in a way that is quite right

definitions.text: the words to describe Kipling's stories
definitions.meaning: the title of Rudyard Kipling's 1902 children's tales of how animals came to be

explanation.surface: Precisely the right phrase for Kipling's tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's collection includes How the Leopard Got His Spots.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase meaning precisely right is also the title of Kipling's fanciful origin stories.

clue.text: Oliver's dance

definitions.meaning: the surname of Dickens's orphan hero
a 1960s dance craze with swivelling hips

explanation.surface: A dance belonging to someone named Oliver.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist is the title character of Dickens's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's orphan bears this surname, which also names Chubby Checker's hip-swivelling dance craze.

clue.text: Horse and a monkey seen in Japanese port

parts.note: a nag is an old horse
the saki is a South American monkey

explanation.surface: A horse and a monkey are spotted in a Japanese harbour city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' and 'seen in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The harbour city on Kyushu, hit by an atomic bomb in 1945, is a major Japanese port.

clue.text: Country had Latin unusually

indicators.note: set out in an unusual way, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A remark that some country unusually used Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges the letters of HAD LATIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The south-east Asian kingdom once called Siam is a nation.

clue.text: Easy perhaps to get a cigarette with marijuana?

definitions.meaning: Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of Captain Marryat's novel

explanation.surface: Asking whether an easygoing person gets a joint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Easy' looks like relaxed; it is the midshipman of Marryat's 1836 novel, and midshipmen were called reefers because they reefed sails. 'to get a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Old naval slang for a midshipman is also slang for a hand-rolled cannabis joint.

clue.text: Wild enthusiasm getting out of order this year

indicators.note: letters out of their proper order are rearranged

explanation.surface: Frenzied excitement has gone out of control this year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of order' rearranges THIS YEAR; 'getting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncontrolled emotional excitement in a crowd is mass frenzy.
